# Maṇicorajātaka (Ja 194)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Jewel Thief

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Maṇicorajātaka* (Ja 194) is a canonical Jātaka tale set during the Buddha's stay at the Veḷuvana monastery, delivered in response to Devadatta's attempts on the Buddha's life [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The Buddha remarks that Devadatta had likewise attempted and failed to destroy him in a past life [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta lives as a virtuous householder in Benares alongside his wife Sujātā [Fausböll 1879; Sujato 2011]. When the corrupt King Brahmadatta becomes enamored of Sujātā, he schemes to have the Bodhisatta falsely accused and executed by planting royal jewels in his cart [Sujato 2011; Tambiah 1976]. As the innocent Bodhisatta faces wrongful death, Sakka intervenes, slays the wicked monarch, and places the Bodhisatta upon the throne [Fausböll 1879; Tambiah 1976]. The story closes with the identification (*samodhāna*): the unrighteous king was Devadatta, Sakka was Anuruddha, Sujātā was Rāhulamātā, and the Bodhisatta became the righteous ruler [Fausböll 1879].

In modern scholarship, the Jātaka is widely cited for its political and environmental doctrines, notably Sakka's declaration that the moral conduct of the ruler governs the natural order [McDermott 1977; Tambiah 1976; Sahni 2008]. If a king is unrighteous, rains fall unseasonably, afflicting the populace with famine, disease, and warfare [McDermott 1977; Sahni 2008; Tambiah 1976]. Scholars like James P. McDermott and Pragati Sahni analyze this narrative alongside the *Kurudhammajātaka* as a prominent canonical precedent for "overflow" or collective karma and early Buddhist environmental ethics [McDermott 1977; Holt et al. 2003; Sahni 2008], while Bhikkhu Sujato highlights its underlying motif of sacred regicide [Sujato 2011].

Regarding text reuse and parallels, DharmaNexus detects six Pali-internal textual matches with the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest §1.1–1.4 matching §745–746) [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
